content: The guidelines, clauses, and limits for bacterial larvicides are similar to those outlined in Sections 4 to 8 of this manual. However, specific differences in requirements and objectives are detailed below. When Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) formulations are proposed for use in drinking water, specifications must include parameters for color, taste, and odor. The maximum acceptable level of microbial contaminants for drinking water or other public health applications has not yet been determined. The active ingredient in bacterial larvicides is described by its genus, species, and strain. If the product is intended for use in drinking water, the description must also include information on its color, odor, and taste. The identity of the active ingredient must be established to ensure the correct bacterial species and strain are used. This includes identifying the internationally recognized culture collection from which reference standard material can be obtained for compliance verification. The content of the active ingredient must be clearly defined, and a method for assaying its biopotency (toxicity to target mosquito species) must be provided. Microbial impurities must be limited to reduce risks associated with handling and to maintain the material's efficacy. Unlike other impurities, microbial contaminants can be introduced during sampling and may increase over time. Sampling and testing must be conducted in specialized facilities by trained personnel. Currently, microbial impurities are assessed on a case-by-case basis by WHO/PCS. Chemical impurities, such as beta-exotoxin, must be limited to prevent adverse effects on non-target organisms. Storage stability is also addressed on a case-by-case basis. For bacterial larvicide technical concentrates (TK), draft specifications must adhere to the guidelines without omitting clauses or introducing more lenient limits unless justified. Notes provided at the end of the guideline should only be incorporated if applicable to the specific specification. The material must consist of the specified genus, species, subspecies, and strain of bacterium, along with related by-products from the manufacturing process. It should be free from visible extraneous matter and added modifying agents, except for stabilizers and free-flow agents if required. The active ingredient must pass an identity test and, if necessary, additional tests to confirm its identity. The active ingredient content, expressed in International Toxic Units (ITU/mg product), must be declared. When tested using the method described, the average biopotency must not be less than 90% of the declared minimum content. The material must be free from beta-exotoxin when tested using the fly larvae toxicity test or an equivalent HPLC method. Water content must meet the maximum allowable limit as determined by the WHO test method. Stability at elevated temperatures is addressed on a case-by-case basis. The biopotency of Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis (Bti) products is compared against a lyophilized reference powder (IPS 82, strain 1884) using early fourth-instar larvae of Aedes aegypti (strain Bora Bora). The toxicity of IPS 82 is assigned an arbitrary value of 15,000 ITU/mg powder. Similarly, the biopotency of Bacillus sphaericus (Bsph) products is determined against a lyophilized reference powder (SPH 88, strain 2362) using early fourth-instar larvae of Culex pipiens pipiens (strain Montpellier). The toxicity of SPH 88 is assigned an arbitrary value of 1,700 ITU/mg powder. The toxicity of all bacterial preparations based on Bti or Bsph can be determined against these standard powders. The toxicity (ITU/mg) of tested products is calculated using a specific formula. Alternative bacterial larvicide reference powders or mosquito strains must be used cautiously, as they may yield different results. Cross-calibration against the reference powders and strains should be conducted by independent expert laboratories, and the data should be made available for verification. For bioassays, reference standard suspensions are prepared by mixing the reference powder with deionized water and a wetting agent. The suspension is homogenized, and aliquots are stored at 4°C for up to one month or frozen at -18°C for up to two years. A stock solution is prepared from the aliquots, and subsequent dilutions are made directly in plastic cups filled with deionized water. Early fourth-instar larvae of Aedes aegypti or Culex pipiens are added to the cups before introducing bacterial suspensions. For products of unknown toxicity, range-finding bioassays are conducted using a wide range of concentrations to estimate approximate toxicity. This information is then used to determine a narrower range of concentrations for more precise bioassays. Mortality is recorded at 24 and 48 hours, depending on the bacterial species tested. For Bti, mortality is typically assessed at 24 hours due to its rapid action, while Bsph preparations are evaluated at 48 hours due to their slower action. Control mortality exceeding 5% requires correction using Abbott’s formula. Tests with control mortality greater than 10% or pupation rates exceeding 5% are invalidated. Dose-response curves are preferably analyzed using statistical programs such as SAS, which incorporate Log Probit Analysis. The toxicity of an unknown preparation is determined by comparing its LC50 value to that of the reference standard. Bioassays should be repeated on at least three different days, and the relative standard deviation (RSD) should be less than 25% for validity. Early fourth-instar larvae are used for testing as they represent the sensitivity of the target population and are convenient to handle. Homogeneous populations of larvae are obtained within five days of hatching using standardized rearing methods. For Aedes aegypti, eggs are laid on filter paper, dried, and stored in sealed plastic bags. When larvae are needed, the paper is immersed in dechlorinated water, and hatching is synchronized by adding larval feed 24 hours prior to egg immersion.
